paras: The assault on Gertrude Ford was an armed threat against a Black woman passenger by a white streetcar conductor in Houston, Texas, in August 1920. After she asked for a transfer, the conductor drew a pistol, threatened to shoot her and forced her off the moving car. Black newspapers in Baltimore, Chicago and Cleveland reported it as one of a series of assaults by armed conductors on Black passengers in the city.

Mrs. Gertrude Ford, of 2170 Tumam [Turman?] Street, was riding the West End-Pierce line when she asked the conductor for a transfer. According to the Baltimore Afro-American, she asked for a transfer or her seven cents back, and the white conductor drew a pistol. The Chicago Defender's correspondent wrote that the conductor cursed her, placed a revolver in her face and threatened to "blow her head off" if she insisted. Both accounts say she was forced to leave the car while it was in motion.

The Defender reported that company officials said that, as she was a "nigger woman," they could offer her only $50 in damages, and that the conductor had not been arrested. No report of an arrest or prosecution of the conductor appears in the coverage.

Only the Black press carried the story, beginning with a short Afro-American brief headlined "Forced Off Moving Car" on August 20 and a fuller Defender story, "Forces Woman to Leap From Street Car," the next day. The Defender stressed the company's slur and the absence of an arrest, while the Cleveland Advocate, under the headline "Houston 'Roughs' Are Looking for Trouble," set the case in a pattern. Its Houston dispatch described a second assault on a Black youth, who would have been shot had a passenger not wrenched the gun from the conductor, and said conductors went armed hoping to shoot Black passengers. No white newspaper report of the incident was found.
The papers differ on the $50: the Defender said the company offered it as damages, while the Afro-American said that Ford offered to settle for fifty dollars.

reader.title: Assault on Gertrude Ford
bases: A single white conductor drew a pistol on a Black woman passenger and threatened to shoot her, forcing her off a moving car; no injury or death is reported (A1, A2).

Three Black papers with differently worded reports and separate Houston datelines agree that a white conductor drew a gun on Mrs. Gertrude Ford after she asked for a transfer (A1, A2, A3); no white-press report was found, and the papers may share a Houston source.

accounts.label: Chicago Defender correspondent
accounts.gist: The conductor cursed Ford, put a revolver in her face, threatened to blow her head off, and forced her to leap from the moving car; the company offered only $50 because she was a 'nigger woman', and the conductor was not arrested.

accounts.label: Baltimore Afro-American brief
accounts.gist: The white conductor drew a pistol when Ford asked for a transfer or her seven cents back and forced her off; Ford offered to settle for $50.

accounts.label: Cleveland Advocate dispatch
accounts.gist: The Ford assault was followed by another on a Black youth, who would have been shot had a passenger not wrenched the gun from the conductor; conductors were said to go armed.

conflicts.note: Neither version is clearly better evidence; the Defender's is longer and more detailed, the Afro-American's is a short brief whose OCR is also garbled.
